# wayland_protocols_misc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-protocols-misc/

## Expand description

This crate provides Wayland object definitions for various orphan or deprecated protocol extensions.

This crate provides bindings for protocols that are generally not officially supported,
but are *de facto* used by a non-negligible number of projets in the wayland ecosystem.

These bindings are built on top of the crates wayland-client and wayland-server.

Each protocol module contains a `client` and a `server` submodules, for each side of the
protocol. The creation of these modules (and the dependency on the associated crate) is
controlled by the two cargo features `client` and `server`.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [gtk_](https://docs.rs/gtk_primary_selection/index.html)- primary_ - selection
- Gtk primary selection protocol
- [server_](https://docs.rs/server_decoration/index.html)- decoration
- KDE server decoration protocol
- [zwp_](https://docs.rs/zwp_input_method_v2/index.html)- input_ - method_ - v2
- Input method v2 unstable
- [zwp_](https://docs.rs/zwp_virtual_keyboard_v1/index.html)- virtual_ - keyboard_ - v1
- Virtual keyboard v1 unstable

---

# wayland-protocols-misc 0.3.12 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wayland-protocols-misc/latest

# wayland-protocols-misc

This crate provides Wayland object definitions for various orphan or deprecated protocol extensions.
It is meant to be used in addition to `wayland-client` or `wayland-server`.

This crate provides bindings for protocols that are generally not officially supported, but are *de facto*
used by a non-negligible number of projects in the wayland ecosystem.

The provided objects are controlled by the `client` and `server` cargo features, which respectively enable
the generation of client-side and server-side objects.

---

# bitflags - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bitflags/^2/

## Expand description

Generate types for C-style flags with ergonomic APIs.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

Add `bitflags` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.bitflags]
version = "2.13.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate features

The `bitflags` library defines a few Cargo features that you can opt-in to:

- `std`: Implement the- `Error`trait on error types used by- `bitflags`.
- `serde`: Support deriving- `serde`traits on generated flags types.
- `arbitrary`: Support deriving- `arbitrary`traits on generated flags types.
- `bytemuck`: Support deriving- `bytemuck`traits on generated flags types.

[§](https://docs.rs#generating-flags-types)Generating flags types

Use the [ bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html) macro to generate flags types:

```
use bitflags::bitflags;
bitflags! {
    pub struct Flags: u32 {
        const A = 0b00000001;
        const B = 0b00000010;
        const C = 0b00000100;
    }
}
```
See the docs for the `bitflags` macro for the full syntax.

Also see the [ example_generated](https://docs.rs/example_generated/index.html) module for an example of what the

`bitflags` macro generates for a flags type.[§](https://docs.rs#externally-defined-flags)Externally defined flags

If you’re generating flags types for an external source, such as a C API, you can define
an extra unnamed flag as a mask of all bits the external source may ever set. Usually this would be all bits (`!0`):

```
bitflags! {
    pub struct Flags: u32 {
        const A = 0b00000001;
        const B = 0b00000010;
        const C = 0b00000100;
        // The source may set any bits
        const _ = !0;
    }
}
```
Why should you do this? Generated methods like `all` and truncating operators like `!` only consider
bits in defined flags. Adding an unnamed flag makes those methods consider additional bits,
without generating additional constants for them. It helps compatibility when the external source
may start setting additional bits at any time. The [known and unknown bits](https://docs.rs#known-and-unknown-bits)
section has more details on this behavior.

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-derives)Custom derives

You can derive some traits on generated flags types if you enable Cargo features. The following libraries are currently supported:

- `serde`: Support- `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]`, using text for human-readable formats, and a raw number for binary formats.
- `arbitrary`: Support- `#[derive(Arbitrary)]`, only generating flags values with known bits.
- `bytemuck`: Support- `#[derive(Pod, Zeroable)]`, for casting between flags values and their underlying bits values.

You can also define your own flags type outside of the [ bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html) macro and then use it to generate methods.
This can be useful if you need a custom

`#[derive]` attribute for a library that `bitflags` doesn’t
natively support:```
#[derive(SomeTrait)]
pub struct Flags(u32);
bitflags! {
    impl Flags: u32 {
        const A = 0b00000001;
        const B = 0b00000010;
        const C = 0b00000100;
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#adding-custom-methods)Adding custom methods

The [ bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html) macro supports attributes on generated flags types within the macro itself, while

`impl` blocks can be added outside of it:```
bitflags! {
    // Attributes can be applied to flags types
    #[repr(transparent)]
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
    pub struct Flags: u32 {
        const A = 0b00000001;
        const B = 0b00000010;
        const C = 0b00000100;
    }
}
// Impl blocks can be added to flags types
impl Flags {
    pub fn as_u64(&self) -> u64 {
        self.bits() as u64
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#renaming-flags)Renaming flags

The [ bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html) macro recognizes a special

`#[bitflags(flag_name = "<value>")]` attribute on flags values to rename them:```
bitflags! {
    pub struct Flags: u32 {
        // Add the attribute to a flag to change its name
        #[bitflags(flag_name = "a")]
        const A = 0b00000001;
        #[bitflags(flag_name = "b")]
        const B = 0b00000010;
        #[bitflags(flag_name = "c")]
        const C = 0b00000100;
    }
}
```
When applied to a flag value, instead of using its identifier, like `A` as the name, it’ll use the given string. This
doesn’t affect the identifier of the constant itself, just the name recognized when parsing and formatting.

[§](https://docs.rs#working-with-flags-values)Working with flags values

Use generated constants and standard bitwise operators to interact with flags values:

```
// union
let ab = Flags::A | Flags::B;
// intersection
let a = ab & Flags::A;
// difference
let b = ab - Flags::A;
// complement
let c = !ab;
```
See the docs for the [ Flags](https://docs.rs/trait.Flags.html) trait for more details on operators and how they behave.

[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-and-parsing)Formatting and parsing

`bitflags` defines a text format that can be used to convert any flags value to and from strings.

See the [ parser](https://docs.rs/parser/index.html) module for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#specification)Specification

The terminology and behavior of generated flags types is
[specified in the source repository](https://github.com/bitflags/bitflags/blob/main/spec.md).
Details are repeated in these docs where appropriate, but is exhaustively listed in the spec. Some
things are worth calling out explicitly here.

[§](https://docs.rs#flags-types-flags-values-flags)Flags types, flags values, flags

The spec and these docs use consistent terminology to refer to things in the bitflags domain:

- **Bits type**: A type that defines a fixed number of bits at specific locations.
- **Flag**: A set of bits in a bits type that may have a unique name.
- **Flags type**: A set of defined flags over a specific bits type.
- **Flags value**: An instance of a flags type using its specific bits value for storage.

```
bitflags! {
    struct FlagsType: u8 {
//                    -- Bits type
//         --------- Flags type
        const A = 1;
//            ----- Flag
    }
}
let flag = FlagsType::A;
//  ---- Flags value
```
[§](https://docs.rs#known-and-unknown-bits)Known and unknown bits

Any bits in a flag you define are called *known bits*. Any other bits are *unknown bits*.
In the following flags type:

```
bitflags! {
    struct Flags: u8 {
        const A = 1;
        const B = 1 << 1;
        const C = 1 << 2;
    }
}
```
The known bits are `0b0000_0111` and the unknown bits are `0b1111_1000`.

`bitflags` doesn’t guarantee that a flags value will only ever have known bits set, but some operators
will unset any unknown bits they encounter. In a future version of `bitflags`, all operators will
unset unknown bits.

If you’re using `bitflags` for flags types defined externally, such as from C, you probably want all
bits to be considered known, in case that external source changes. You can do this using an unnamed
flag, as described in [externally defined flags](https://docs.rs#externally-defined-flags).

[§](https://docs.rs#zero-bit-flags)Zero-bit flags

Flags with no bits set should be avoided because they interact strangely with [ Flags::contains](https://docs.rs/trait.Flags.html#method.contains)
and

[. A zero-bit flag is always contained, but is never intersected. The names of zero-bit flags can be parsed, but are never formatted.](https://docs.rs/trait.Flags.html#method.intersects)

`Flags::intersects`[§](https://docs.rs#multi-bit-flags)Multi-bit flags

Flags that set multiple bits should be avoided unless each bit is also in a single-bit flag. Take the following flags type as an example:

```
bitflags! {
    struct Flags: u8 {
        const A = 1;
        const B = 1 | 1 << 1;
    }
}
```
The result of `Flags::A ^ Flags::B` is `0b0000_0010`, which doesn’t correspond to either
`Flags::A` or `Flags::B` even though it’s still a known bit.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [iter](https://docs.rs/iter/index.html)
- Yield the bits of a source flags value in a set of contained flags values.
- [parser](https://docs.rs/parser/index.html)
- Parsing flags from text.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- Generate a flags type.
- [bitflags_](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags_match.html)- match
- A macro that matches flags values, similar to Rust’s `match`statement.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- A defined flags value that may be named or unnamed.

# wayland_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-client/^0.31.14/

## Expand description

Interface for interacting with the Wayland protocol, client-side.

[§](https://docs.rs#general-concepts)General concepts

This crate is structured around four main objects: the [ Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html) and

[structs, proxies (objects implementing the](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html)

`EventQueue`[trait), and the](https://docs.rs/trait.Proxy.html)

`Proxy`[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`The [ Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html) is the heart of this crate. It represents your connection to the Wayland server, and
you’ll generally initialize it using the

[method, which will attempt to open a Wayland connection following the configuration specified by the ! environment.](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html#method.connect_to_env)

`Connection::connect_to_env()`Once you have a [ Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html), you can create an

[from it. This](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html)

`EventQueue`[will take care of processing events from the Wayland server and delivering them to your processing logic, in the form of a state struct with several](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html)

`EventQueue`[implementations (see below).](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`Each of the Wayland objects you can manipulate is represented by a struct implementing the [ Proxy](https://docs.rs/trait.Proxy.html)
trait. Those structs are automatically generated from the wayland XML protocol specification. This crate
provides the types generated from the core protocol in the

[module. For other standard protocols, see the](https://docs.rs/protocol/index.html)

`protocol``wayland-protocols` crate.[§](https://docs.rs#event-dispatching)Event dispatching

The core event dispatching logic provided by this crate is built around the [ EventQueue](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html) struct. In
this paradigm, receiving and processing events is a two-step process:

- First, events are read from the Wayland socket. For each event, the backend figures out which `EventQueue`
- Then, the `EventQueue``Dispatch::event()``State`value that was provided to it.

The main goal of this structure is to make your `State` accessible without synchronization to most of
your event-processing logic, to reduce the plumbing costs. See [ EventQueue](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html)’s documentation for
explanations of how to use it to drive your event loop, and when and how to use multiple
event queues in your app.

In this paradigm, your `State` needs to implement `Dispatch<O, _>` for every Wayland object `O` it needs to
process events for. This is ensured by the fact that, whenever creating an object using the methods on
an other object, you need to pass a [ QueueHandle<State>](https://docs.rs/struct.QueueHandle.html) from the

[that will be managing the newly created object.](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html)

`EventQueue`However, implementing all those traits on your own is a lot of (often uninteresting) work. To make this
easier a composition mechanism is provided using the [ delegate_dispatch!](https://docs.rs/macro.delegate_dispatch.html) macro. This way, another
library (such as Smithay’s Client Toolkit) can provide generic

[implementations that you can reuse in your own app by delegating those objects to that provided implementation. See the documentation of those traits and macro for details.](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started-example)Getting started example

As an overview of how this crate is used, here is a commented example of a program that connects to the
Wayland server and lists the globals this server advertised through the `wl_registry`:

```
use wayland_client::{protocol::wl_registry, Connection, Dispatch, QueueHandle};
// This struct represents the state of our app. This simple app does not
// need any state, but this type still supports the `Dispatch` implementations.
struct AppData;
// Implement `Dispatch<WlRegistry, ()> for our state. This provides the logic
// to be able to process events for the wl_registry interface.
//
// The second type parameter is the user-data of our implementation. It is a
// mechanism that allows you to associate a value to each particular Wayland
// object, and allow different dispatching logic depending on the type of the
// associated value.
//
// In this example, we just use () as we don't have any value to associate. See
// the `Dispatch` documentation for more details about this.
impl Dispatch<wl_registry::WlRegistry, ()> for AppData {
    fn event(
        _state: &mut Self,
        _: &wl_registry::WlRegistry,
        event: wl_registry::Event,
        _: &(),
        _: &Connection,
        _: &QueueHandle<AppData>,
    ) {
        // When receiving events from the wl_registry, we are only interested in the
        // `global` event, which signals a new available global.
        // When receiving this event, we just print its characteristics in this example.
        if let wl_registry::Event::Global { name, interface, version } = event {
            println!("[{}] {} (v{})", name, interface, version);
        }
    }
}
// The main function of our program
fn main() {
    // Create a Wayland connection by connecting to the server through the
    // environment-provided configuration.
    let conn = Connection::connect_to_env().unwrap();
    // Retrieve the WlDisplay Wayland object from the connection. This object is
    // the starting point of any Wayland program, from which all other objects will
    // be created.
    let display = conn.display();
    // Create an event queue for our event processing
    let mut event_queue = conn.new_event_queue();
    // And get its handle to associate new objects to it
    let qh = event_queue.handle();
    // Create a wl_registry object by sending the wl_display.get_registry request.
    // This method takes two arguments: a handle to the queue that the newly created
    // wl_registry will be assigned to, and the user-data that should be associated
    // with this registry (here it is () as we don't need user-data).
    let _registry = display.get_registry(&qh, ());
    // At this point everything is ready, and we just need to wait to receive the events
    // from the wl_registry. Our callback will print the advertised globals.
    println!("Advertised globals:");
    // To actually receive the events, we invoke the `roundtrip` method. This method
    // is special and you will generally only invoke it during the setup of your program:
    // it will block until the server has received and processed all the messages you've
    // sent up to now.
    //
    // In our case, that means it'll block until the server has received our
    // wl_display.get_registry request, and as a reaction has sent us a batch of
    // wl_registry.global events.
    //
    // `roundtrip` will then empty the internal buffer of the queue it has been invoked
    // on, and thus invoke our `Dispatch` implementation that prints the list of advertised
    // globals.
    event_queue.roundtrip(&mut AppData).unwrap();
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-use)Advanced use

It may be that for some of your objects, handling them via the [ EventQueue](https://docs.rs/struct.EventQueue.html) is impractical. For example,
if processing the events from those objects doesn’t require accessing some global state, and/or you need to
handle them in a context where cranking an event loop is impractical.

In those contexts, this crate also provides some escape hatches to directly interface with the low-level
APIs from `wayland-backend`, allowing you to register callbacks for those objects that will be invoked
whenever they receive an event and *any* event queue from the program is being dispatched. Those
callbacks are more constrained: they don’t get a `&mut State` reference, and must be threadsafe. See
[ Proxy::send_constructor()](https://docs.rs/trait.Proxy.html#tymethod.send_constructor) and

[for details about how to assign such callbacks to objects.](https://docs.rs/backend/trait.ObjectData.html)

`ObjectData`[§](https://docs.rs#interaction-with-ffi)Interaction with FFI

It can happen that you’ll need to interact with Wayland states accross FFI. A typical example would be if
you need to use the [ raw-window-handle](https://docs.rs/raw-window-handle/) crate.

In this case, you’ll need enable the `system` feature to use the `libwayland` backend of
`wayland-backend`.

- If you need to send pointers to FFI, you can retrive the `*mut wl_proxy`pointers from the proxies by first getting the`ObjectId``Proxy::id()``ObjectId::as_ptr()`

# wayland_protocols - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-protocols/^0.32.12/

## Expand description

This crate provides bindings to the official wayland protocol extensions
provided in [https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/wayland/wayland-protocols](https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/wayland/wayland-protocols)

These bindings are built on top of the crates wayland-client and wayland-server.

Each protocol module contains a `client` and a `server` submodules, for each side of the
protocol. The creation of these modules (and the dependency on the associated crate) is
controlled by the two cargo features `client` and `server`.

[§](https://docs.rs#protocol-categories)Protocol categories

The protocols provided in this crate are grouped in 4 main categories:

- The `wp`
- The `xdg`
- The `xwayland`
- The `ext`

[§](https://docs.rs#staging-protocols)Staging protocols

The cargo feature `staging` enables the generation of the staging protocols.

These protocols are ready for wider adoption and clients and compositors are encouraged to implement staging protocol extensions where a protocol’s functionality is desired.

Although these protocols should be stable, the protocols may still be completely replaced in a new major version or with a completely different protocol.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-protocols)Unstable protocols

The `wayland-protocols` project previously had a notion of “unstable protocols” representing protocols
that are still being worked on and evolving. These protocols are recognized by the use of the prefix `z`
in their interface names.

This category has now been deprecated and is no longer supposed to be used, however several protocols
are still under that umbrella. We can expect them to be replaced by staging and stable protocols in the
long term, but in the meantime you can enable them with the `unstable` cargo feature.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-protocols)Other protocols

Additionally, more protocol extensions are provided here:

---

# wayland_scanner - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-scanner/^0.31.10/

## Expand description

Wayland protocol code-generation machinnery

This crate provides procedural macros for generating the rust code associated with a
Wayland XML protocol specification, for use with the `wayland-client`, `wayland-server`
and `wayland-backend` crates.

Before trying to use this crate, you may check if the protocol extension you want to use
is not already exposed in the `wayland-protocols` crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-usage)Example usage

Below is a template for generating the code for a custom protocol client-side. Server-side
is identical, just replacing `client` by `server`. The path to the XML file is relative to the
crate root.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// Generate the bindings in their own module
pub mod my_protocol {
    use wayland_client;
    // import objects from the core protocol if needed
    use wayland_client::protocol::*;
    // This module hosts a low-level representation of the protocol objects
    // you will not need to interact with it yourself, but the code generated
    // by the generate_client_code! macro will use it
    pub mod __interfaces {
        // import the interfaces from the core protocol if needed
        use wayland_client::protocol::__interfaces::*;
        wayland_scanner::generate_interfaces!("./path/to/the/protocol.xml");
    }
    use self::__interfaces::*;
    // This macro generates the actual types that represent the wayland objects of
    // your custom protocol
    wayland_scanner::generate_client_code!("./path/to/the/protocol.xml");
}
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [generate_](https://docs.rs/macro.generate_client_code.html)- client_ - code
- Proc-macro for generating client-side API associated with an XML specification
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/macro.generate_interfaces.html)- interfaces
- Proc-macro for generating low-level interfaces associated with an XML specification
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/macro.generate_server_code.html)- server_ - code
- Proc-macro for generating server-side API associated with an XML specification

# wayland_server - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wayland-server/^0.31.13/

## Expand description

Interface for interacting with the Wayland protocol, server-side.

[§](https://docs.rs#general-concepts)General concepts

This crate is structured around four main objects: the [ Display](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html) and

[structs, resources (objects implementing the](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayHandle.html)

`DisplayHandle`[trait), and the](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html)

`Resource`[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`The [ Display](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html) is the heart of this crate, it represents the protocol state of your Wayland server, and
takes care of processing messages from clients. You’ll need to integrate it in your event loop (see its
documentation for details). From it you can retrieve the

[, which is a clonable handle to the Wayland state and is the type used to actually interact with the protocol.](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayHandle.html)

`DisplayHandle`Each of the Wayland object you can manipulate is represented by a struct implementing the [ Resource](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html)
trait. Thos structs are automatically generated from the wayland XML protocol specification. This crate
provides the types generated from the core protocol in the

[module. For other standard protocols, see the](https://docs.rs/protocol/index.html)

`protocol``wayland-protocols` crate.The request dispatching logic provided by this crate is build around the [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html) trait. During the
dispatching process (in

[), all requests sent by clients are read from their respective process and delivered to your processing logic, by invoking methods on the various](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html#method.dispatch_clients)

`Display::dispatch_clients()`[implementations of your](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch``State` struct. In this paradigm, your `State` needs to implement
`Dispatch<O, _>` for every Wayland object `O` it needs to process events for.However, implementing all those traits on your own is a lot of (often uninteresting) work. To make this
easier a composition mechanism is provided using the [ delegate_dispatch!()](https://docs.rs/macro.delegate_dispatch.html) macro. This way, another
library (such as Smithay) can provide generic

[implementations that you can reuse on your own app by delegating those objects to that provided implementation. See the documentation of those traits and macro for details.](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)

`Dispatch`[§](https://docs.rs#globals)Globals

The entry point of the protocol for clients goes through the protocol globals. Each global represents a
capability of your compositor, a peripheral it has access to, or a protocol extension it supports.
Globals are created by you using [ DisplayHandle::create_global()](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayHandle.html#method.create_global), and require your

`State` to
implement the [trait for the interface associated with that global.](https://docs.rs/trait.GlobalDispatch.html)

`GlobalDispatch`[§](https://docs.rs#logging)Logging

This crate can generate some runtime error message (notably when a protocol error occurs). By default
those messages are printed to stderr. If you activate the `log` cargo feature, they will instead be
piped through the `log` crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-use)Advanced use

It may be that for some of your objects, handling them via the [ Dispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html) trait is impractical. In
those contexts, this crate also provides some escape-hatches to directly interface with the low-level
APIs from

`wayland-backend`, allowing you to register callbacks for those objects by directly providing
implementations of the backend [trait. See](https://docs.rs/backend/trait.ObjectData.html)

`ObjectData`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html#method.create_resource_from_objdata)

`Client::create_resource_from_objdata()`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.DataInit.html#method.custom_init)

`DataInit::custom_init()`[§](https://docs.rs#interaction-with-ffi)Interaction with FFI

It can happen that you’ll need to interact with Wayland states accross FFI, such as for example when interfacing with the graphics stack for enabling hardware acceleration for clients.

In this case, you’ll need enable the `system` feature to use the `libwayland` backend of
`wayland-backend`.

Then, you’ll generally need:

- The `*mut wl_display`pointer, that you can retrieve by first retrieving the`Backend``Display::backend()``.handle()``.display_ptr()`
- The `*mut wl_resource`pointers for the objects you need to share, by first getting the`ObjectId``Resource::id()``ObjectId::as_ptr()`

If you need to receive pointers from FFI, you can make [ ObjectId](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.ObjectId.html)s from the

`*mut wl_resource` pointers
using [, and then make the resources using](https://docs.rs/backend/struct.ObjectId.html#method.from_ptr)

`ObjectId::from_ptr()`[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html#tymethod.from_id)

`Resource::from_id()`## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [delegate_](https://docs.rs/macro.delegate_dispatch.html)- dispatch
- A helper macro which delegates a set of `Dispatch``Dispatch`
- [delegate_](https://docs.rs/macro.delegate_global_dispatch.html)- global_ - dispatch
- A helper macro which delegates a set of `GlobalDispatch``GlobalDispatch`

- [Client](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html)
- A struct representing a Wayland client connected to your compositor.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataInit.html)- Init
- Helper to initialize client-created objects
- [Display](https://docs.rs/struct.Display.html)
- The Wayland display

- A handle to the Wayland display
- [Listening](https://docs.rs/struct.ListeningSocket.html)- Socket
- An utility representing a unix socket on which your compositor is listening for new clients
- [New](https://docs.rs/struct.New.html)
- A newly created object that needs to be initialized. See `DataInit`

- The `ObjectData`
- [Weak](https://docs.rs/struct.Weak.html)
- A weak handle to a Wayland object

- Error that can occur when trying to bind a `ListeningSocket`
- [Dispatch](https://docs.rs/enum.DispatchError.html)- Error
- An error generated if an illegal request was received from a client
- [WEnum](https://docs.rs/enum.WEnum.html)
- An enum value in the protocol.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Dispatch](https://docs.rs/trait.Dispatch.html)
- A trait which provides an implementation for handling a client’s requests from a resource with some type of associated user data.
- [Global](https://docs.rs/trait.GlobalDispatch.html)- Dispatch
- A trait which provides an implementation for handling advertisement of a global to clients with some type of associated user data.
- [Resource](https://docs.rs/trait.Resource.html)
- Trait representing a Wayland interface

# wayland_protocols_misc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/wayland-protocols-misc/latest/target-redirect/wayland_protocols_misc/

## Expand description

This crate provides Wayland object definitions for various orphan or deprecated protocol extensions.

This crate provides bindings for protocols that are generally not officially supported,
but are *de facto* used by a non-negligible number of projets in the wayland ecosystem.

These bindings are built on top of the crates wayland-client and wayland-server.

Each protocol module contains a `client` and a `server` submodules, for each side of the
protocol. The creation of these modules (and the dependency on the associated crate) is
controlled by the two cargo features `client` and `server`.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [gtk_](https://docs.rs/gtk_primary_selection/index.html)- primary_ - selection
- Gtk primary selection protocol
- [server_](https://docs.rs/server_decoration/index.html)- decoration
- KDE server decoration protocol
- [zwp_](https://docs.rs/zwp_input_method_v2/index.html)- input_ - method_ - v2
- Input method v2 unstable
- [zwp_](https://docs.rs/zwp_virtual_keyboard_v1/index.html)- virtual_ - keyboard_ - v1
- Virtual keyboard v1 unstable

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# moorage 0.0.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/moorage/0.0.1

# moorage

Install your self-authored agent **skills and plugins** into one central home, and
wire every agent harness to them from a single source of truth. A small Rust CLI.

*(Renamed from  skilldock, which collided on GitHub.)*

## Commands

```
moorage install   SOURCE [--mode dev|normal] [--skills a,b] [--harnesses claude,pi,omp,codex]
                         [--force] [--dry-run] [--no-post-install]
moorage uninstall NAME... [--dry-run]
moorage update    NAME... [--force] [--dry-run]
moorage list
moorage doctor    [--json]
```
All commands accept the six root overrides (see *Roots* below). `--dry-run` prints the
full action plan — skills, links, hook placements, registration merges, backups,
post_install — and mutates nothing.

## Skills (no manifest — behavior unchanged)

`SOURCE` may be a directory containing `SKILL.md` (single skill) or a repo with
`skills/*/SKILL.md` (multi-skill; scanned one level). The skill **name** comes from
the `SKILL.md` frontmatter `name:` and must be lowercase `[a-z0-9-]`, ≤ 64 chars,
with a non-empty `description:` (pi's discovery rule — enforced so the link name is
correct). A `skills/*` layout is **preferred** over a repo-root `SKILL.md`, so a repo
carrying both installs its `skills/<name>` payloads (the baseline shape).

Each skill installs to `~/.moorage/skills/{name}`:

| Mode | `~/.moorage/skills/{name}`is | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `dev`(default) | a symlink to the repo payload | authoring / iterating |
| `normal`(alias:`local`) | a real copy (excludes `.git`,`__pycache__`) | pinned snapshot |

and the agent roots link into the home:

```
~/.agents/skills/{name}  --+                              +-- dev:    repo payload (live)
                           +-->  ~/.moorage/skills/{name} -+
~/.claude/skills/{name}  --+                              +-- normal: a copy in the home
```
oh-my-pi reads both locations; all agents dedupe by real path.

## Plugins (`moorage.toml` manifest)

A `moorage.toml` at the repo root (or passed directly as `SOURCE`) upgrades a repo to
a plugin. **Its absence changes nothing** — no-manifest repos keep the exact behavior
above.

```
 = "conversate"          # optional plugin label (names placed hook files)
[]                    # optional preferences (see Precedence)
 = "dev"                 # dev | normal | local
 = ["claude", "pi", "omp", "codex"]
[[]]
 = "."                   # payload dir, repo-root-relative ("." = repo root)
 = "normal"              # optional per-skill override
 = ["claude"]       # optional per-skill override
[[]]
 = "hooks/claude/settings-snippet.json"   # merged into <claude-root>/settings.json
[[]]
 = "hooks/pi/conv-turn-counter.ts"         # placed into <pi-root>/agent/extensions/
[[]]
 = "hooks/pi/conv-turn-counter.ts"         # placed into <omp-root>/hooks/{stage}/
 = "pre"                                    # default "pre" when omitted
[[]]
 = "hooks/codex/hooks.json"                # merged into <codex-root>/hooks.json
[]
 = ["python scripts/example.py init"]         # optional; cwd = canonical skill dir
```
### Preference precedence

`CLI flags > per-skill entry > [install] table > built-in defaults` (mode `dev`, all
four harnesses). `--mode` / `--harnesses` on the command line mean "override the
manifest". The `harnesses` list gates both the skill links (`claude` → claude-root
link; any of `pi`/`omp`/`codex` → agents-root link) and the hook wiring per harness.
Per-skill `harnesses` gate that skill's links; plugin-level hooks follow
`CLI > [install] > default`.

### Hook FILES (pi, omp)

Placed as **file symlinks** named `moorage-{label}-{basename}` (label = manifest
`name`, else the first skill's name) pointing at the canonical copy inside
`~/.moorage/skills/{name}/...` — so dev/normal switching is transparent. If file
symlinks are unavailable (Windows without Developer Mode) the file is **copied** with
a loud warning, and doctor tracks drift of copied placements. Junctions are dir-only
and hardlinks die across volumes, so neither is used for files. Hook scripts must
live inside a `[[skills]]` payload (otherwise no canonical home copy exists — the
install refuses that hook).

### Registration MERGES (claude, codex)

The snippet's `hooks` block merges into the target config via a serde_json
round-trip that preserves unrelated keys:

- claude → `<claude-root>/settings.json`
- codex → `<codex-root>/hooks.json`(plus a printed reminder that codex loads hooks only with`[features] hooks = true`in`~/.codex/config.toml`— moorage**never**edits that file)

Merges are **append-if-absent** (exact-equality dedupe ⇒ idempotent re-installs), and
a syntactically invalid target config is refused, never clobbered. Before the
**first** modification of each config, a `.bak` copy goes into `~/.moorage/backups/`
(named `{basename}.{epoch}.bak`, recorded in state).

**Command-path rewriting** (design ruling; the v2 exact rule is unrecovered): every
whitespace-separated token of a `command` / `commandWindows` string that resolves —
relative to an installed skill payload root — to an existing file is rewritten to the
absolute path of that file under the canonical home
(`~/.moorage/skills/{name}/...`). The **home** path, never the source repo path, so
dev-mode symlinks keep the loop live. Rewritten paths containing spaces are quoted; a
token that itself contains spaces can never match (whitespace split — a known v2
limitation). Snippets should therefore reference their scripts by payload-relative
paths (e.g. `hooks/claude/counter.ps1`).

### Reversibility

Every inserted JSON entry is persisted **verbatim** in `state.toml` *and* is
self-marked by containing the `~/.moorage/skills/{name}` path in its command (no
marker keys are injected — that would fight harness schema validation). `uninstall`:

- unmerges exactly the recorded entries (falling back to the home-path marker for
entries a user edited in place); emptied configs are left as `{}`, never deleted;
- removes placed hook files and agent links (links are dropped, targets untouched);
- removes the home entry — for dev mode the **symlink only**, never the target repo;
- deletes the state record.

Source repositories are never touched. Legacy state records (pre-plugin, five fields)
still load; uninstalling one derives the two conventional agent-link paths and
deletes each **only after verifying it actually points into the moorage home** —
anything else is skipped with a warning.

### post_install

Commands run after all components are placed, with `cwd` = the canonical skill dir in
the home (first skill for multi-skill plugins). Each command is echoed and its
outcome recorded in state. `--no-post-install` skips them (recorded as `skipped`). A
failing command **reports loudly, marks the state record ( failed(N)), sets exit
code 1, and does NOT roll back the install** (design ruling — fix the cause and
re-run, or uninstall).

`update` never runs post_install.## update

- **dev**installs: verify and repair the whole chain — home link, agent links, hook files; re-apply merges when snippets changed (stale recorded entries are unmerged, new ones merged; stale hook files removed).
- **normal**installs: hash-compare (in-crate FNV-1a-64 over the payload tree) and re-copy- **only if the source changed**;- **refuse**when the installed copy was hand-edited (or when a legacy record has no stored hash to verify against) —- `--force`overrides.

## doctor

Read-only, always. Checks: state.toml parse health; full chain integrity (agent link
→ home → payload); dangling/re-targeted links; placed hook files (missing, dangling,
copy drift vs canonical); merged registrations (recorded entries still present,
target configs valid); **orphaned** moorage-marked entries (home path in the command
but absent from state); unmanaged entries (reported, never touched) incl. pi
name-rule violations; shadowing (same name under claude-root and agents-root
resolving to different real paths); normal-mode content drift vs source; dev-mode git
hygiene (dirty tree, non-main branch — best effort); manifest preference drift
(manifest prefers a different mode than installed); `AGENTS.md` inside a skill dir
(pi issue #2473). `--json` emits the findings machine-readably. Exit code is 0 even
with findings; nonzero means doctor itself failed to run.

## Conflicts, idempotency, dry-run

- An entry already resolving to the right target is left alone (idempotent re-runs); merges dedupe by exact equality.
- A conflicting foreign entry is **refused**with a clear message;`--force`renames it to a sibling`{name}.bak-N`and replaces it.
- `--dry-run`prints the full plan and changes nothing (configs are only read).

## Roots (for tests / alternate setups)

Flag > env > default, uniformly:

| Setting | Flag | Env | Default | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| home | `--home` | `MOORAGE_HOME` | `~/.moorage` | canonical home, state, backups |
| agents root | `--agents-root` | `MOORAGE_AGENTS_ROOT` | `~/.agents` | pi/omp/codex skill links |
| claude root | `--claude-root` | `MOORAGE_CLAUDE_ROOT` | `~/.claude` | Claude skill links + `settings.json`merges |
| pi root | `--pi-root` | `MOORAGE_PI_ROOT` | `~/.pi` | hook files under `agent/extensions/` |
| omp root | `--omp-root` | `MOORAGE_OMP_ROOT` | `~/.omp` | hook files under `hooks/{stage}/` |
| codex root | `--codex-root` | `MOORAGE_CODEX_ROOT` | `~/.codex` | `hooks.json`merges |

## state.toml

`~/.moorage/state.toml` records, per skill: `name`, `mode`, `source`, `installed`/
`updated` (epoch secs), and — for plugin installs — `plugin` label, `manifest` path,
effective `harnesses`, `home_kind` (symlink/junction/copy), `copy_hash` (normal
mode), `[[links]]` (path/kind/target), `[[hook_files]]` (path/kind/target),
`[[merges]]` (file/event/verbatim entry), `[[post_install]]` (command/status), and
`[[backups]]` (original/backup). Legacy five-field records load unchanged.

## Windows link fallback

Directory links try: real symlink (needs Developer Mode or elevation) → NTFS
**junction** via `cmd /c mklink /J` (no privileges) → **copy** with a loud warning.
File placements try: file symlink → copy (drift tracked by doctor). On non-Windows,
symlinks are used directly.

## Unverified upstream paths (honesty notes)

- **omp**: upstream documents only- *project-level*- `.omp/hooks/{stage}/*.ts`discovery. The user-level- `<omp-root>/hooks/{stage}/`placement is a- **best-documented-guess**(unverified upstream). doctor emits a- `warn`note when omp hook files are installed; override with- `--omp-root`.
- **codex**: whether codex reads a- *user-level*- `hooks.json`at all is- **unverified**(only project-level- `.codex/hooks.json`is documented). doctor emits a- `warn`note when codex merges are installed; override with- `--codex-root`.
- **pi**(- `~/.pi/agent/extensions`) and- **claude**(- `~/.claude/settings.json`) are documented/known paths.

## Design rulings (unrecovered v2 details, decided here)

- **Command rewriting token rule**: whitespace token → resolve against installed payload roots (manifest order, first match) → rewrite to the absolute canonical home path; quote only when the result contains spaces; absolute tokens skipped.
- **Mode name**: the CLI keeps- `dev|normal`;- `local`(the v2 name) is accepted as an alias both on the CLI and in manifests.
- **omp**:- `stage`default- `"pre"`(the only value ever observed).
- **post_install failure**: loud warning +- `failed(N)`in state + exit 1, no rollback;- `--no-post-install`records- `skipped`;- `update`never runs post_install.
- `--force`backups- `{name}.bak-N`convention (the pinned minimal-Rust behavior) instead of moving into- `~/.moorage/backups/`; the backups dir holds config- `.bak`snapshots only, named- `{basename}.{epoch}.bak`.
- **backups/ contents are permanent**: uninstall does not delete taken backups (traceability).
- **Multi-skill plugins**: post_install cwd = first skill's canonical dir; hook artifacts are named after the manifest- `name`(else the first skill); the plugin component ledger (hook files, merges, post_install, backups) rides on the first skill's state record.
- **Manifests must declare**: a manifest with no skills entry is an error (hooks need a payload to live in).- `[[skills]]`
- **Corrupt state.toml**: mutating commands refuse to run over an unparseable ledger (protecting the live records); doctor reports it as a- `fail`finding.
- `update`flags- `--force`(attested) plus- `--dry-run`(inferred-carried).
- **Content hashing**: in-crate FNV-1a-64 (stable across releases, zero deps) — std's- `DefaultHasher`is explicitly not used for persisted hashes.

## Build

```
cargo build --release          # binary at target/release/moorage(.exe)
cargo install --path .         # optional: install to ~/.cargo/bin
```
Tests: `cargo test` (unit: manifest parse, merge/unmerge/rewrite, state round-trip
incl. legacy records) and `python -m pytest tests/ -q` (29 black-box tests against
the built binary with all six roots pinned to temp dirs; set `MOORAGE_BIN` to point
at a specific exe, else `target/debug/moorage`).

Requires a stable Rust toolchain. Dependencies: `clap` (CLI), `serde` + `toml`
(manifests + state), `serde_json` (registration merges).

---

# polkadot_jemalloc_shim - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-jemalloc-shim/0.6.0/polkadot_jemalloc_shim/

## Expand description

Shim crate to enable `jemalloc-allocator` feature for Polkadot crates.

Because [there doesn’t exist any easier way right now](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/1197), we
need an entire crate to handle `jemalloc` enabling/disabling. This way we can enable it by
default on Linux, but have it optional on all other OSes.

# sim_lib_sound_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-sound-core/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_sound_core/

## Expand description

Core sound primitives for the SIM music constellation.

This crate defines the foundational acoustic types shared by the
sound/synthesis layer: [ Frequency](https://docs.rs/struct.Frequency.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/struct.Amplitude.html)

`Amplitude`[quantities; the](https://docs.rs/struct.Phase.html)

`Phase`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Partial.html)

`Partial`[, and](https://docs.rs/struct.Envelope.html)

`Envelope`[models that build a spectral tone from sinusoidal components; and helpers for default envelopes and equal-temperament pitch-to-frequency conversion.](https://docs.rs/struct.Tone.html)

`Tone`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Amplitude](https://docs.rs/struct.Amplitude.html)
- A non-negative linear amplitude.
- [Envelope](https://docs.rs/struct.Envelope.html)
- An attack/decay/sustain/release amplitude envelope.
- [Frequency](https://docs.rs/struct.Frequency.html)
- A positive frequency in hertz.
- [Partial](https://docs.rs/struct.Partial.html)
- A single sinusoidal component of a tone.
- [Phase](https://docs.rs/struct.Phase.html)
- A phase angle in radians.
- [Tone](https://docs.rs/struct.Tone.html)
- A complete tone: a set of `Partial``Envelope`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Envelope](https://docs.rs/enum.EnvelopeShape.html)- Shape
- The interpolation curve applied across an `Envelope`
- [Sound](https://docs.rs/enum.SoundCoreError.html)- Core - Error
- Error raised when sound primitives are constructed with invalid values.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_envelope.html)- envelope
- Returns a general-purpose default envelope (short attack and decay, high sustain, moderate release, linear shape).
- [equal_](https://docs.rs/fn.equal_temperament_frequency.html)- temperament_ - frequency
- Returns the 12-tone equal-temperament frequency of `pitch`, with A4 (MIDI 69) anchored at 440 Hz.

# vize_fresco - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/vize_fresco/0.273.0/vize_fresco/

## Expand description

Fresco - Vue TUI Framework

A high-performance Terminal User Interface framework for Vue.js, similar to React Ink but built with Rust for performance.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- **Terminal Control**: Cross-platform terminal handling via crossterm
- **Flexbox Layout**: Layout engine powered by taffy
- **CJK Support**: Full Unicode text handling including Japanese IME
- **Efficient Rendering**: Double-buffered differential rendering

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Vue Components                        │
│                  (Box, Text, Input)                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  Vue Custom Renderer                     │
│                    (TypeScript)                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   NAPI Bindings                          │
│             (Rust <-> Node.js bridge)                    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
        ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
        ▼                 ▼                 ▼
┌───────────────┐ ┌───────────────┐ ┌───────────────┐
│   Terminal    │ │    Layout     │ │    Render     │
│   (backend,   │ │   (taffy,     │ │   (tree,      │
│    buffer)    │ │    flex)      │ │    diff)      │
└───────────────┘ └───────────────┘ └───────────────┘
        │                                   │
        ▼                                   ▼
┌───────────────┐                 ┌───────────────┐
│     Input     │                 │     Text      │
│  (keyboard,   │                 │   (width,     │
│   mouse, ime) │                 │    segment)   │
└───────────────┘                 └───────────────┘
```

# vize_musea - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/vize_musea/0.273.0/vize_musea/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#vize_musea)vize_musea

Musea - Component gallery and documentation for Vize.

[§](https://docs.rs#name-origin)Name Origin

**Musea** (plural of museum) represents a gallery space where art is
displayed and documented. Similarly, `vize_musea` provides a gallery
for Vue components, allowing developers to view and interact with
components in isolation - similar to Storybook.

[§](https://docs.rs#concepts)Concepts

- **Art**: A component variation/state (replaces “story”)
- **Art file**(- `*.art.vue`): File defining arts
- **Gallery**: Display area for arts
- **Palette**: Interactive controls panel

[§](https://docs.rs#performance)Performance

This crate is optimized for high performance:

- **Zero-copy parsing**: All strings are borrowed from source
- **Arena allocation**: Uses- `vize_carton::Bump`for fast allocation
- **Minimal allocations**: Only allocates when absolutely necessary
- **Fast byte-level parsing**: Uses- `memchr`and- `memmem`for O(n) search

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

```
use vize_carton::Bump;
use vize_musea::{parse_art, transform_to_csf};
use vize_musea::types::ArtParseOptions;
let allocator = Bump::new();
let source = r#"
<script setup lang="ts">
defineArt("./Button.vue", { title: "Button" });
</script>
<art>
  <variant name="Primary" default>
    <Button variant="primary">Click me</Button>
  </variant>
  <variant name="Secondary">
    <Button variant="secondary">Click me</Button>
  </variant>
</art>
"#;
// Parse Art file with arena allocator
let art = parse_art(&allocator, source, ArtParseOptions::default()).unwrap();
// Transform to Storybook CSF
let csf = transform_to_csf(&art);
println!("Generated: {}", csf.filename);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- Zero-copy parsing of `*.art.vue`files
- Type-safe variant definitions
- Storybook CSF 3.0 export
- Visual Regression Testing (VRT) support
- Interactive props palette

# vize_atelier_sfc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/vize_atelier_sfc/0.273.0/vize_atelier_sfc/

## Expand description

Vue Single File Component (.vue) compiler.

This module provides parsing and compilation of Vue SFCs, following the Vue.js core structure:

- `parse`- SFC parsing into descriptor blocks
- `compile_script`- Script/script setup compilation
- `compile_template`- Template block compilation (DOM and Vapor)
- `compile`- Main SFC compilation orchestration
- `style`- Style block compilation with scoped CSS
- `css`- Low-level CSS compilation with LightningCSS

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use vize_atelier_sfc::{parse_sfc, compile_sfc, SfcParseOptions, SfcCompileOptions};
let source = r#"
<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
const count = ref(0)
</script>
<template>
  <button @click="count++">{{ count }}</button>
</template>
"#;
let descriptor = parse_sfc(source, SfcParseOptions::default()).unwrap();
let result = compile_sfc(&descriptor, SfcCompileOptions::default()).unwrap();
println!("{}", result.code);
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use bundler::`- [BundlerCustomBlock](https://docs.rs/bundler/struct.BundlerCustomBlock.html);
- `pub use bundler::`- [BundlerStyleBlock](https://docs.rs/bundler/struct.BundlerStyleBlock.html);
- `pub use bundler::`- [SfcBlockAttribute](https://docs.rs/bundler/struct.SfcBlockAttribute.html);
- `pub use bundler::`- [SfcSrcInfo](https://docs.rs/bundler/struct.SfcSrcInfo.html);
- `pub use bundler::`- [TemplateAssetTagRule](https://docs.rs/bundler/struct.TemplateAssetTagRule.html);
- `pub use bundler::`- [TemplateAssetUrl](https://docs.rs/bundler/struct.TemplateAssetUrl.html);
- `pub use bundler::`- [collect_template_asset_urls](https://docs.rs/bundler/fn.collect_template_asset_urls.html);
